title: For the ones who chose
hook: a blessing for the righteous, the pious and sincere converts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing against harm, and Beruriah's let sins cease. Your line was end the harm. Did you aim your anger at the deed, not the person? Today, the blessing that comes right after it, for the good. Day five hundred ninety.

Around the year 1200, a man named Obadiah, who had become a Jew, writes a worried letter to the most famous rabbi alive, Moses Maimonides, in Egypt. His question is about the Amidah. Every day, it begins: our God and God of our fathers, God of Abraham. But Obadiah's fathers weren't Abraham's children. Should he change the words? Say God of your fathers? He's afraid he's telling a small lie three times a day. Maimonides' answer is still read today.
screen: `A LETTER TO MAIMONIDES.` → `GOD OF OUR FATHERS?` → `A SMALL LIE THREE TIMES A DAY?`

segments.voice: Maimonides writes back: say it exactly as written. Abraham is your father too. He's the father of everyone who comes under the wings of the Divine Presence. Converts are often named son or daughter of Abraham and Sarah for this reason. And then, in the thirteenth blessing of the Amidah, the community prays for them by name. It says: on the righteous, on the pious, on the elders of Your people, on the remnant of their scholars, on the righteous converts, and on us, may Your compassion be stirred. Give good reward to all who truly trust in Your name, and place our portion with them. Blessed are You, support and trust of the righteous. Look at that list. The converts, gerei hatzedek, stand right next to the righteous and the scholars. And notice the last item: and on us. The ordinary person praying adds themselves at the end of the list, hoping to belong in that company. The Torah tells Israel more than once to love the stranger, the ger, a word that later also came to mean a convert. In the old Jewish translation: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." And the most famous convert of all, Ruth, says to Naomi: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Her great-grandson is King David. In this blessing, the people who chose stand at the very center of the community's prayer.
screen: `MAIMONIDES: ABRAHAM IS YOUR FATHER.` · `THE RIGHTEOUS, THE PIOUS, THE CONVERTS.` · `AND ON US.` · `RUTH: THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.` · then, large: `FOR THE ONES WHO CHOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone who chose this path. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who chose to join a people, a family or a community they weren't born into. Maybe a convert you know. Maybe an in-law who learned all the family recipes, or a neighbor who became a citizen. Think of what it cost them: the learning, the questions, the moments of feeling outside. Hold them with respect for a few breaths. If you pray, you can include them in this blessing. The bell holds the time.
For the ones who chose. The Amidah's thirteenth blessing, for the righteous, the pious, the scholars, the righteous converts, and us.
screen: `FOR THE ONES WHO CHOSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for the ones who chose. Today, tell the person you pictured one specific thing you admire about how they joined in. Day five hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Al hatzaddikim is the thirteenth blessing of the weekday Amidah, praying for the righteous, the pious, the elders, the scholars and righteous converts; converts to Judaism say the Amidah with the same words, God of our fathers.

original.note: Hebrew: righteous converts. ger first meant a stranger living among the people.

trapdoor: what you thought: a blessing for good people in general.
what it means: a prayer that puts converts beside the righteous and the scholars, and adds us at the end.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides' letter to Obadiah the proselyte; Deuteronomy 10:19; ger as resident stranger in the Bible and convert in rabbinic Hebrew.
